title: Replace Excel with custom software when your spreadsheet becomes your bottleneck
content_html:
Your team has been using the same Excel file for two years. Three people edit it every day. The formulas are so tangled that only one colleague understands them. When that person is on holiday, nothing gets updated. You have asked yourself: is there software that does this? The answer is usually yes. But the real question is whether an off-the-shelf tool, a low-code platform, or custom software is the right fit.

This article walks through the signs that your spreadsheet has outgrown itself, and the honest trade-offs between your three options.

The spreadsheet has become a bottleneck when these things happen

A spreadsheet stops being a working document and starts being a problem when the team's workflow depends on it, but the spreadsheet itself gets in the way. The most common signs are these.

Multiple people edit the same file at the same time, and changes collide or overwrite each other. You have moved to a shared drive or cloud storage to reduce the chaos, but the chaos is still there. Another sign is that data lives in three different sheets, and someone manually copies numbers from one sheet to another every day. A third is that the file has grown so large that it takes minutes to open or recalculate. A fourth is that you have built manual checks into the workflow because you do not trust the formulas. You ask a team member to spot-check the totals by hand before you send the file to the accountant or the client.

The deepest sign is this: the spreadsheet works only because one person knows how it works. That person has built the formulas, named the ranges, and documented nothing. If that person leaves or takes a long holiday, the team loses the ability to use the file reliably. You cannot hire someone new and train them in an afternoon.

When one or more of these patterns fit your team, the spreadsheet has stopped being a tool and has become a liability.

Three honest options: package, low-code, or custom

Once you have decided to move away from the spreadsheet, you have three paths. Each has real strengths and real limits.

Off-the-shelf software packages solve a known problem for many teams. Accounting software, project management tools, CRM systems. These packages come with workflows that somebody else has already designed. You do not have to build anything. The cost is low and predictable. The downside is that your team's process probably does not match the package's workflow exactly. You will have to change how you work, or you will spend months configuring the package to fit you. If the package does not fit your process, and changing your process is not worth it, then a package is the wrong choice.

Low-code platforms sit in the middle. Tools like Mendix and OutSystems let you build an application without writing code from scratch. You can model your exact workflow. The platform handles the technical plumbing. The catch is that low-code platforms still require someone on your team to learn the platform, design the data model, and build the workflows. That takes weeks or months. You also own the maintenance and updates. If your team does not have someone who wants to learn the platform, low-code becomes a stalled project.

Custom software is built specifically for your workflow. A developer or a team of developers writes the code. You do not have to change how you work. The software follows your process. The trade-off is time and cost upfront. Custom software takes longer to build than a package, and it costs more than low-code. But when your process is genuinely different from what a package offers, custom software is often the only way to get something that actually works for you.

How to decide which path is right for you

Start by testing whether an off-the-shelf package fits. If your workflow is standard, a package will save you time and money. [Why Standard Project Controls Software SaaS Misses the Mark for Growing Teams](/en/insights/why-standard-project-controls-software-saas-misses-the-mark) walks through when packages fail and when they work.

If a package does not fit, and you have someone on the team who enjoys building and learning technical tools, low-code might work. If you do not, or if your process is too specific, custom software is the honest choice.

When you are ready to explore custom software, the first step is a scoping phase. This is a three-week paid project where a developer sits with your team, maps your current workflow, and documents what the software needs to do. At the end, you have a clear specification and a go-or-no-go decision. You are not locked in. You could take that specification to another supplier if you wanted to. This phase is how you decide whether custom software is worth building at all.
